newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Stubborn British inflation refuses to fall.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Stubborn British inflation refuses to fall.

text.p: Underlying British inflation stuck fast at 3.3 percent in the year to November, putting pressure on Prime Minister John Major's embattled Conservative government to ratchet up interest rates.
The Office for National Statistics said on Thursday that retail price inflation, excluding volatile home loan payments, edged up by 0.1 percent in the month, leaving the year-on-year rate unchanged.
Headline inflation also crept up by 0.1 percent and was unmoved at 2.7 percent year-on-year.
Economic secretary to the Treasury Angela Knight put a brave face on the numbers, saying high street prices would soon start to fall as lower producer prices feed through to retailers.
"We are continuing to achieve the best inflation performance for 30 years and inflation on the high street should soon benefit from factory gate inflation at 30-year lows," she said.
Figures released earlier this week showed producer output prices rose only 0.8 percent in the year to November -- the lowest rate of increase since 1967.

The government has set itself a target of 2.5 percent for underlying inflation and with elections approaching within five months, Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke will not be keen to put up interest rates to help reach that goal.
The opposition Labour Party said Thursday's figures showed inflation remains unconquered.
"John Major described last month's inflation figures as a statistical aberration," said Labour Treasury spokesman Alan Milburn. "Today's news makes a mockery of that claim."
When underlying inflation rose to a year-on-year 3.3 percent in October from 2.9 in September, the government said the low level of inflation in October 1995 exaggerated the rise.

The Confederation of British Industry cast another cloud over the outlook for factory gate prices on Thursday. Its monthly survey of British manufacturing firms showed an increasing number expecting higher prices.

"The pick-up expected in domestic prices is now becoming more firmly based, suggesting that a turning point in output price inflation is at hand," said Sudhir Junankar, associate director of economic analysis at the CBI.
Economists were uncertain retail prices would fall again.

"Today's data give the lie to the government's assertion that October's rise was a blip," said Marian Bell, economist at the Royal Bank of Scotland. "Nor do we forecast significantly lower inflation from next month on."
Nonetheless, Clarke did not take the opportunity to increase base rates following Wednesday's meeting with Bank of England Governor Eddie George, leaving them unchanged at six percent.
Thursday morning money market operations by the Bank of England, conducted at an unchanged rate, confirmed that.

Economists said Clarke would have seen the retail price inflation figures before the meeting. "The Chancellor runs the risk of inflicting larger and more freqent hikes in rates the longer he leaves this one," Bell said.

Economists are concerned that retailers, who have seen their profit margins squeezed for several years as consumers refused to swallow higher prices, might now take the opportunity offered by buoyant high street demand to push prices higher.
Alex Garrard, UK economist at UBS, said the breakdown of Thursday's inflation figures showed prices rising fastest in those areas where demand is strongest.
Clothing and footwear prices shot up by 1.1 percent last month, the highest November rise in more than 20 years, while household goods prices rose by 1.0 percent.
